articles.title: UK’s Healey says government will fill defense plan gap by ‘reprioritizing’
articles.snippet: Finance minister John Healey said on Wednesday "reprioritization" in other departments would fill a £4.7 billion ($6.3 billion) gap in Britain's Defence Investment Plan.
articles.full_text:
LONDON — Finance minister John Healey said on Wednesday “reprioritization” in other departments would fill a £4.7 billion ($6.3 billion) gap in Britain’s Defence Investment Plan, a blueprint government hopes shows its NATO commitment.
In his first budget, Healey said he would also adopt this approach of “looking hard at public spending” to set out the details of how Britain will meet the NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035, and mark a target date for 3% in 2030.
“In today’s budget, I am fully funding the Defence Investment Plan, including through capital reprioritization across Whitehall. This honors the commitment made both by me – and by the prime minister,” he told parliament, referring to a part of London home to most government departments.
Healey, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Defense Minister Wes Streeting are under pressure to increase investment more quickly.
Confirming that detailed plans for reaching the 3% and 3.5% goals will be set out in a spending review planned next year, Healey said he was also “determined to use more innovative financing, alongside the private sector and our international allies.”
That delay in plotting a clear pathway to 3.5% will heighten calls by the main opposition Conservatives, who have demanded Healey’s resignation if he failed to set out a credible plan at the budget.
Healey resigned as defense minister under Keir Starmer in June over what Healey viewed as inadequate spending on defense, specifically over the former prime minister’s unwillingness or inability to find funds to reach the 3% goal by 2030.

articles.title: Finlands defense minister talks NATO, Ukraine and fishing
articles.snippet: "We know that Russia is a threat, but we have to just do our stuff, be prepared to invest heavily, keep our friends close, get new friends globally and do stuff right —that’s the Finnish way to handle a difficult security situation."
articles.full_text:
Finland’s Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen visited New Zealand on Oct. 21 to discuss security issues with officials there. His travel agenda also included Australia and Japan, signaling the Northern European country’s interest in the region despite the geographical distance.
“We are reinforcing our relations with partners in the Indo-Pacific region. In addition, we see plenty of opportunities to deepen defense materiel cooperation,” Häkkänen was quoted as saying in a statement released by the Finnish government ahead of the trip.
He caught up with Defense News in Wellington for a brief interview.
What NATO assets is Finland prepared to host?
When we joined NATO we were prepared, nationally, to defend ourselves. As a NATO member our first responsibility is a strong, national defense with lots of European assets in the Navy, Air Force and also in space nowadays.
We have established NATO’s northern Europe’s land headquarters in the Arctic area, on Finnish soil. So we are leading the land defense.
What are your priorities for Finland’s defense?
We have four pillars in our defense policy. The first one is that Finland, by itself, has to be always, always, ready to defend our own country.
Second, is strong NATO in northern Europe. Now we have built NATO’s capabilities to operate in Arctic areas, so we are really happy to see that NATO’s evermore able to act in the north.
Third, is defense corporation with different countries. Some countries — for example the United States and European countries — are in operational planning on how to act together in crisis situations, so that’s the third pillar. Supporting NATO’s Article five.
And the fourth pillar is comprehensive security. We have to have enough from our own country: energy, food, equipment from the defense industry. We have civil shelters for almost 5.5 million people [editor’s note: much of Finland’s total population], and the whole society has to be prepared to act in crisis mode. Every company has to plan how they can operate, even if war starts.
We are developing and investing heavily in those pillars. The Finnish way to do things is cost-effective, high-quality and win-win. We are not just saying that Finland needs something, we’re also ready to provide our knowledge, our expertise.
How do your NH90 operations compare with New Zealand’s?
There were difficulties at the start. But now our special forces and our land forces are using the NH90 and they have been customized to Finnish needs, to our special environment. Our pilots are really satisfied and when they have compared NH90 to some other equipment that is now in the market, they think that this is still the best one.
How is Finland supporting Ukraine ?
Heavily, by all the political levels. We are heavy supporters of Ukrainian military from our stocks. We are giving a lot of money, because we see that if Ukraine doesn’t stop Russia, Russia’s hunger will grow for Europe and they will do something nasty.
Supporting Ukraine is also supporting our own security and it shows all the other dictators around the world that democratic nations are united to support Ukraine and oppose violence against neighbors. That’s why we are really happy to see that New Zealand’s also [supporting] Ukraine.
France has offered to extend its nuclear deterrent to Europe, what do you think of that proposal ?
Let me be clear, NATO’s nuclear deterrence comes [from] U.S. weapon systems, that’s for sure, but France gives an additional, extra deterrence and that will create some strategic dilemmas for Putin.
What keeps you awake at night ?
My kids! I have two small kids and I live at the eastern border, at the Russian border, so I’m cool. I fish there, in beautiful lakes, and I have my house there with my family, so I’m taking it easy, like everyone who lives [there]. That’s a strong border.
We have always tried to have diplomatic relations with Russia, but throughout history, from Catherine the Great to Peter the Great, Russians have always been willing to use violence, against their own people, but also against their neighbors.
That’s why Finland has been always pragmatic in defense and security, you have to always be ready. That’s why we are so cool and calm. There [are] a million reservists in Finland, everyone has had military training. We know that Russia is a threat, but we have to just do our stuff, be prepared to invest heavily, keep our friends close, get new friends globally and do stuff right —that’s the Finnish way to handle a difficult security situation.
The Joint Expeditionary Force, is that proving useful?
JEF is one of the most important defense operations for Finnish and northern Europe’s defense. We think that the most valuable part of JEF is that it can react fast; JEF has already operated, so there’s no need to wait for some kind of clear Article Five case.
How can New Zealand’s forces support yours?
Well, we are now having this dialogue between our partners … there’s different kinds of possibilities with different organizations. For example, today we discussed space capabilities, Finland has a lot of space companies and a lot of technological expertise, but New Zealand has different kinds of space capability, launching, for example. Also countering problems with undersea cables.
Do you see Ukraine joining NATO?
Maybe someday. Ukraine’s path is to the West, to their democratic alliances in Europe. But all the NATO countries have to approve it and U.S. and other countries have said no at this point.
About a quarter of New Zealand’s defense force consists of women, do you know the percentage of women in Finland’s forces?
It’s much smaller, but it’s rising. All the men are obliged to participate and it’s voluntary for women. The number of women are growing now because everyone in Finland wants to participate.
Is everyone still happy in Finland?
Yeah, we’re the happiest nation in the world, for nine years in a row. Even though there’s some challenges and dark clouds in the war in Europe, still people in Finland are quite cool.
Russia is building new military infrastructure near our borders, so we have to do more for our security. But we can do it, it’s not a big problem.
I’m optimistic. The Finnish mindset … it’s kind of a mixup of reason and optimism. You face the world as it is. You have to adapt, take your chances, find the possibilities in economy, security and do the best that you can do.

articles.title: If Canada picks the Gripen fighter, these local firms would help Saab deliver the jets
articles.snippet: Saab will collaborate with several of Canada’s top aerospace firms to build the Gripen fighter jet in Canada if the aircraft is selected by the Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.
articles.full_text:
VICTORIA, British Columbia — Saab will collaborate with several of Canada’s top aerospace firms to build the Gripen fighter jet in Canada if the aircraft is selected by the Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government.
Saab confirmed Oct. 27 that it has formed alliances with several firms to build, deliver and support the Gripen E advanced multi-role fighter, should the Canadian government purchase the plane.
Canada had already committed to buying 88 Lockheed Martin F-35s but that is under review after U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to economically cripple the country and suggested it could be annexed to be the 51st state. At this point Canada has paid for 16 F-35s.
Two of the aircraft were transferred to Canada on Oct. 9 and Oct. 22, said Department of National Defence spokeswoman Andrée-Anne Poulin.
Canadian Prime Minister Carney will decide whether the rest of the F-35s will be purchased but he has not indicated when he would announce his decision.
In the meantime, the Canadian government is examining whether it should purchase the Gripen E, either as an alternative to the F-35 or to complement the U.S. fighter jets. Saab has responded by forming a teaming arrangement with Canadian firms CAE of Montreal, Quebec; IMP of Halifax, Nova Scotia; and Magellan Aerospace of Mississauga, Ontario.
“Together with CAE, IMP and Magellan Aerospace we are prepared to establish a strong Canadian industrial ecosystem around Gripen that delivers operational effect, national sovereignty and lasting industrial and technological benefits,” Micael Johansson, President and CEO of Saab, said in a statement Oct. 27.
Saab noted it has signed a teaming agreement with IMP to establish a new final assembly line, for the Gripen fighter in Canada, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft. IMP will also be responsible for electrical assembly production and in-service support for Canada’s Gripens.
Saab has also signed a new Memorandum of Understanding with Magellan Aerospace to provide local manufacturing of advanced aerostructures, composite structures and structural assemblies in Canada — again, if Canada decides to acquire the aircraft.
Saab has previously signed a Memorandum of Understanding with CAE to deliver advanced fighter pilot and technician training, mission systems engineering and support/sustainment capabilities in Canada.
Saab has already made significant inroads into the Canadian market.
Carney announced May 27 that Canada will purchase six GlobalEye early warning and control aircraft from Saab as part of deal to not only boost Canadian military capabilities but energize domestic defense production.
Carney said the proposed GlobalEye purchase is estimated to cost more than $5 billion CAN ($3.6 billion).
GlobalEye is based on a Bombardier 6500 executive jet, an aircraft that is manufactured in Toronto. Carney said that at least one-third of the projected GlobalEye aircraft orders for various allies will be built in Canada. That is expected to be 40 aircraft over the next 15 years.
On Sept. 25 the Canadian government announced it had worked out an agreement with Saab that will provide the framework for upcoming negotiations on the purchase of the six GlobalEyes.
In announcing the agreement, Stephen Fuhr, Secretary of State for Defence Procurement, said Canada will be focusing on pursuing a partnership that supports “Canadian jobs, innovation, and long-term economic growth while ensuring we acquire capabilities from trusted partners when they are needed.”

articles.title: US Air Force awards Lockheed Martin $694M hypersonic missile production contract
articles.snippet: The Air Force granted Lockheed Martin a $694 million contract in late September for the production and fielding of the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force awarded Lockheed Martin a nearly $700 million contract for the production and fielding of a hypersonic missile.
The service granted Lockheed the $694 million contract in late September as it moved the AGM-183A Air-Launched Rapid Response Weapon, or ARRW, from prototyping and flight testing to production, according to a Monday announcement.
“This is a turning point in our advanced weapons roadmap,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink, said in a release. “By moving ARRW from test to production, we’re providing our combatant commanders with a credible, high-speed strike weapon capable of penetrating the most advanced anti-access and area-denial systems.”
The contract, which was completed under the Defense Department’s Enterprise-Wide Agile Acquisition Contract, is another effort by the U.S. military to modernize the country’s Arsenal of Freedom, the statement says.
The ARRW is designed to accelerate to speeds greater than Mach 5 by using a solid-fuel rocket booster before releasing a hypersonic glide vehicle. The boost-glide hypersonic missile is meant to give the service the ability to strike heavily defended targets from a safe distance away, or standoff range, in a time-sensitive manner, the announcement states.
“Fielding ARRW enhances our ability to hold targets at risk anywhere around the world,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach said in the release. “This hypersonic weapon provides the Joint Force a flexible and rapid response option for highly contested environments.”
The announcement did not say how many missiles Lockheed is expected to produce or specify its timeline for delivery, citing operational security risks.
The Air Force previously moved to halt the purchase of ARRWs in 2023 after its prototyping phase ended, following unsuccessful tests, and instead opted to focus on its other major hypersonic weapon program, the Hypersonic Attack Cruise Missile.
Then, two years later in 2025, the service’s then-Chief of Staff Gen. David Allen told Congress that the service intends to revitalize its ARRW program with new funding in the fiscal 2026 budget proposal after not including it in the fiscal 2025 budget request.
The service allotted roughly $387 million for the ARRW program in its fiscal 2026 procurement budget request, according to budget documents. For fiscal 2027, the Air Force boosted the program’s budget slightly with a request for $452 million, budget documents show.

articles.title: Pentagon creates advisory council on human performance, health
articles.snippet: After creating a new directorate on warfighter optimization within the Department of Defense, the Pentagon announced it will form a federal advisory committee to weigh in on issues affecting troop performance and health.
articles.full_text:
After creating a new directorate on warfighter optimization within the Department of Defense, the Pentagon announced it will form a federal advisory committee to weigh in on issues affecting troop performance and health.
According to a Federal Register notice Tuesday, the $1.4 million committee will focus “exclusively on human performance,” providing guidance and insight on improving function, combating the physical, mental and emotional tolls of military service known collectively as “operator syndrome,” and preventing physical injuries and operational stress.
“The Council will serve as a high-impact, low-cost mechanism for the [DoD] to secure the expertise of the nation’s foremost leaders at the nexus of warrior health and performance,” the announcement stated.
The Pentagon established a Warfighter Performance Optimization division earlier this year within Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata’s office. It is intended to oversee and coordinate the individual services’ efforts to improve troops’ readiness and performance.
In May, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed Tata to report on existing optimization initiatives across the services to create a department-wide performance optimization plan.
Hegseth said he wanted to accelerate fielding technologies that will improve performance — such as wearable devices and other analytics tools — and focus on elevating “cognitive performance as a key to readiness.”
“By building on and modernizing the principles of Total Force Fitness (TFF), WPO will deliver a unified operational approach to accelerate readiness, dominance, and peak performance across the Force. We will treat the Warfighter as a readiness capability, held to the same disciplined evaluation, maintenance, and optimization we demand of every asset that preserves combat power,” Hegseth wrote.
The services have created their own approaches to health, fitness and human performance within the last several years. Army introduced its Holistic Health and Fitness initiative in 2020 to improve the health of the force and reduce the number of soldiers considered non-deployable because of chronic medical conditions.
The Navy introduced its Human Performance Optimization program as a pilot in San Diego in February, providing training and education on nutrition, sleep, injury prevention and stress management.
The Marine Corps has had a total fitness strategy since 2023 that combines wellness, fitness, mental health and data to improve the health of members, while the Air Force is building a new human performance optimization facility at Davis-Monthan Air Force Base in Arizona, which is designed to support Air Force Special Warfare airmen.
The new advisory committee will have up to 20 members with expertise in an array of scientific and medical fields, including urology, endocrinology, nutrition, neurology, combat stress, orthopedics, preventive medicine, wearable technology or spiritual, psychiatric or psychological health, sleep medicine and human factors engineering.
As with all federal advisory committees, volunteers are unpaid and only receive travel pay and per diem reimbursement when conducting council-related business.
The announcement described the council as “an exceptionally cost-effective resource.”
The newly formed group, the announcement stated, will provide information that helps the services create “lethal, operationally ready warriors prepared physically, psychologically, for successful large-scale, high kinetic, combat operations against peer adversaries who are imbued with the essential Warrior Ethos to win decisively,” the announcement stated.
Shortly after Hegseth took office last year, he dismissed the members of roughly 40 Defense Department advisory boards and launched reviews to determine whether they supported his goal to “revive the warrior ethos” in the U.S. armed forces.
The Defense Advisory Committee on Women in the Services and the Defense Advisory Committee for the Prevention of Sexual Misconduct were among those terminated.
Hegseth has also created several new advisory boards since being sworn in, most recently, the Homeland Defense Board, announced Sept. 11, which he plans to chair. The board will provide guidance on military support for homeland security missions.

articles.title: US Army queries industry’s ability to build 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles
articles.snippet: The U.S. Army published a market survey Monday in an effort to learn whether the defense industrial base could deliver 9,000 ISV-9s and about 12,000 ISV-Us.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army is asking whether the defense industrial base can deliver and support nearly 21,000 Infantry Squad Vehicles.
An Army market survey published Monday focuses on two ISV versions: the ISV-9, which carries nine passengers, and the ISV-Utility, which carries five passengers plus a utility bed to haul cargo.
“The estimated total requirement is for 20,787 vehicles (9,003 ISV-9 and 11,784 ISV-U), subject to fund availability and requirements from the U.S. Army, other sister services and potential Foreign Military Sales (FMS) customers,” the survey said.
“To ensure the most streamlined, competitive, and cost-effective approach, the government is utilizing the results of this market survey to determine the feasibility of several procurement pathways.”
The ISV, from GM Defense, is based on General Motors’s commercial Colorado and Silverado pickups. GM Defense was awarded a $697.7 million contract modification last month for engineering changes to the ISV-U and the ISV-U Utility Winch Kit, bringing the cumulative value to $915.6 million.
GM Defense announced Oct. 12 that the Army expanded orders for the ISV from an initial 649 to nearly 12,000.
In the market survey, contractors are asked to provide the Army with manufacturing cost estimates based on “varying annual production volumes (e.g., 100, 500, 1,000, and 1,500+ units per year) to evaluate economy-of-scale thresholds.”
The survey also includes a timeline that begins in fiscal 2028 with an acquisition of 106 vehicles. The acquisition continues to fiscal 2036, with the Army receiving around 2,000 to 2,100 vehicles per year.
The survey also listed numerous technical specifications. The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have a maximum vehicle curb weight of 5,200 pounds, plus an operational payload of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-9 and a payload capacity of 5,000 pounds for the ISV-U. Both versions will have a gross vehicle weight rating of up to 10,200 pounds, the survey said.
Both vehicles require baseline military modifications, including blackout lights, 24V electrical systems, main power disconnect, run-flat tires, the ability to ford both salt and fresh water, MIL-STD-814/MIL-STD-209K life and tie-down provisions, 24V NATO slave receptacles on the front and rear bumper, an integrated winch and Military Petroleum, Oils, and Lubricants (POL) compatibility.”
The ISV-9 and ISV-U will have full rollover protection for their passengers. The ISV-U will also have a winch, a 4,000-watt inverter with multiple electrical outlets, towing capacity of up to 6,500 pounds and the capability to carry “non-ambulatory patients as a kit.”
The vehicles should be capable of traveling up to 55 miles per hour on good paved roads and 17 miles per hour cross country.
“Both the ISV-9 and ISV-U shall be capable of traversing longitudinal grades up to 60% and must reliably meet stringent mobility profile requirements across improved, secondary, and un-improved surfaces (trails and cross-country) without fatiguing the occupants when the platform is operating at GVW [gross vehicle weight],” the Army said.

articles.title: Canadian firms line up for potential GCAP, Gripen work
articles.snippet: Back in July, the Italian Ministry of Defense told Breaking Defense that at that stage, being an observer did not entail that Canada had an industrial role in GCAP, adding that it was infeasible then “to predict the timing, modalities, or conditions of any potential expansion” of the country’s new participation.
articles.full_text:
MILAN — Canadian companies announced plans this week to team up with European partners on a pair of continental defense programs — assuming Ottawa moves forward with either of them.
Montreal-based aerospace manufacturer Bombardier signed a Memorandum of Understanding today with Britain’s BAE Systems “to collaborate toward next-generation combat air programs,” the two companies said in a press release. While not spelling it out in the release, the phrase “next-generation combat air” is a clear reference to Canada’s potential tie-up with the British-Japanese-Italian Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP).
While the announcement offered few details on what this initial partnership will entail, it said the parties aimed to identify which technological sectors and capabilities made the most sense for them to cooperate on.
“This MoU marks an important step in exploring how Bombardier’s aerospace expertise, advanced manufacturing capabilities and defense integration experience could contribute to the development of next-generation air combat capabilities,” the company said in its press release.
In July, Canada’s government announced it was joining GCAP as an observer. At the time, the Italian Ministry of Defense told Breaking Defense that, at that stage, being an observer did not entail that Canada had an industrial role in GCAP, adding that it was infeasible then “to predict the timing, modalities, or conditions of any potential expansion” of the country’s new participation.
Since then, there has been little new information about Ottawa’s role in the sixth-generation fighter. But Canadian industry is certainly optimistic about getting involved in what could become a major global fighter aircraft.
On the sidelines of the Farnborough International Airshow over the summer, Pascal Grenier, the president of Defense and Security at Canada’s leading flight simulation and training company CAE, said that he hoped that Ottawa’s observer status within GCAP could pave the way for new opportunities for the Canadian aerospace industry.
Saab Sweetens The Pot
Meanwhile, Tuesday brought an announcement from Swedish firm Saab, which revealed three major Canadian industrial partners it will bring on board should Ottawa move forward with acquiring the Gripen fighter.
“Saab confirms its intention to collaborate with several of Canada’s major international aerospace firms in a first step to establish a broad, national ecosystem that will build, deliver and support the Gripen E should the Canadian government proceed with a Gripen acquisition,” the Swedish company said.
The Saab proposal envisions producing and finally assembling the Gripen in Canada. It signed an agreement with Halifax-based IMP to oversee a new Canadian final assembly line and electrical production; another one with Magellan Aerospace to locally produce aerostructures and composite structures; and a final agreement with CAE to deliver pilot and technician training as well as mission systems engineering.
Canada’s planned purchase of 72 additional F-35s from Lockheed Martin — after confirming an initial order for 16 aircraft — has been under review since March 2025. This has left open the possibility of a mixed fleet, which could include Saab-made Gripen jets, a move the company has lobbied hard for in Canada.
In July, Canadian Defense Minister David McGuinty told reporters that the decision status had not moved and would remain under consideration “until we take the time to get it right for Canadians.”

articles.title: UK commits to 3 percent GDP on defense by 2030, new investment partnerships with industry
articles.snippet: Chancellor John Healey said that the UK’s recent Defence Investment Plan would be “fully” funded, indicating the money for defense would come from cuts to other priorities.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The United Kingdom plans to reach 3 percent GDP spending on defense by 2030, Chancellor John Healey announced today as part of a broader budget announcement that also indicated a greater partnership with the defense industry to come.
In a speech today, Healey said that the UK’s recent Defence Investment Plan would be “fully” funded, indicating the money for defense would come from cuts to other priorities.
In addition, he said that next year’s spending review would spell out exactly how the UK plans to hit the NATO commitment of spending 3.5 percent GDP on defense by 2035, and how the UK will be at 3 percent by 2030.
That the news came from Healey added extra oomph for defense watchers.
Healey was defense secretary under previous Prime Minister Keir Starmer before publicly resigning over what Healey described as underfunding the military. That resignation triggered several others, which ultimately pushed Starmer to resign and be replaced by Burnham — who then brought Healey back as his main financial officer.
Other defense-related announcements in budget documents released with Healey’s speech today include:
- The standup of a new Innovative Defence Financing Taskforce to “maximise the contribution of private and international finance to UK defence;”
- The opening of discussions with Finland, Poland and the Netherlands to pool funding for “defence investment and joint procurement across NATO allies”;
- A plan for the “National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank to deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use and other sectors that support our national security, sovereign capability and resilience;”
- The creation of a Ministry of Defence-led “drone regulation unit” which will work across different agencies to cut” red tape and create clearer routes for testing uncrewed and autonomous systems,” which would seem to mirror some of the concerns about regulation authorities over UAVs in the United States.
- £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in additional funds for Ukraine.
- The government has a currently-unfunded plan for a 10-year, £2.5 billion program with Rolls-Royce to develop a next-gen gas turbine engine that would be dual-use. “This has not been contracted and funding is subject to award, negotiations and relevant legal processes,” per the documents.

articles.title: How General Atomics views Europe’s unmanned future
articles.snippet: In this fireside chat, Dave Alexander of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems talks through his company’s strategy for the European market.
articles.full_text:
The future of European airpower is very much up in the air, but it is clear that unmanned capabilities will play a major role going forward.
In this fireside chat, Breaking Defense Editor-in-Chief Aaron Mehta sits down with Dave Alexander, the president of General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, to discuss his views on the European market, what kind of industrial partnerships he looks for, and what a European CCA may do differently than an American one.
You can find the previous episodes of our European airpower roundtable here and at Breaking Defense Europe.

articles.title: Navy faces ‘years-long’ maintenance crunch amid record-breaking, extended deployments
articles.snippet: Extended deployments in the Middle East could compound existing maintenance delays, with Navy leaders warning that returning ships will strain shipyard capacity and force trade-offs between repairs and modernization.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The US Navy expects it will take years for its fleet to recover from recent drawn out deployments, with leaders bracing for a surge in maintenance work that could strain shipyard capacity and force trade-offs between repairs and modernization.
Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said Monday that the service is bracing for maintenance availabilities — particularly impacting the destroyer fleet — to snowball as some of its aircraft carriers and surface vessels return from more than 300-day long periods at sea. As a result, the Navy is weighing how to prioritize repairs, shorten some timelines and defer larger projects without pushing the service’s schedule further behind.
“You’re talking hundreds of availabilities and millions of dollars. Hundreds of millions of dollars have to be applied to that problem as we start retrograding these destroyers back into their maintenance period,” Caudle said at the United States Navy Memorial. “But this is a years-long recovery. There is no workaround on that.”
Speaking earlier this month, Vice Chief of Naval Operations Adm. James Kilby voiced similar concerns, noting that efforts in the Middle East like Operation Epic Fury have contributed to “artificially high combat surge ready rates” because ships remain at sea on extended deployments and have yet to return from the region. However, he warned that “the problem will come when they eventually do come home,” signaling that an influx of ships entering maintenance could postpone modernization efforts.
“The industrial base will not be able to swallow that pill, and so we’ll have to sequence that,” Kilby said during an Oct. 8 National Commission on the Future of the Navy hearing. “There’s a couple things that can happen there. I’ll defer maintenance. I’ll either squish the package into the bare minimum and not do modernization things I need to do. So that’s the bill that’s being paid there.”
This year, extended deployments have pushed the Navy’s ships well beyond their typical seven-month period at sea. For example, the aircraft carrier Gerald R. Ford completed a 326-day deployment in May — shattering the aircraft carrier Abraham Lincoln’s previous record of 294 days at sea in 2019 and 2020.
Destroyers have also logged exceptionally long deployments this year. The McFaul returned to Naval Station Norfolk on Oct. 23 after an 11-month deployment totaling 332 days at sea. While underway, the ship integrated with the Abraham Lincoln, George H.W. Bush and the George Washington carrier strike groups to provide anti-air warfare and surface fire support amid combat operations, the Navy said in a news release.
The destroyer Spruance has been at sea even longer. The San Diego Union-Tribune reported that the destroyer surpassed the record for longest destroyer deployment after the ship hit 339 days underway on Sunday, a milestone previously held by a destroyer in World War II.
A Navy spokesperson told Breaking Defense in July that the service has 75 destroyers in its fleet. More than a dozen destroyers are actively deployed in the Red Sea and Arabian Sea as of Monday, according to the USNI News fleet tracker.
While the public shipyards typically conduct maintenance for nuclear-powered submarines and aircraft carriers, private yards usually oversee repairs for the Navy’s surface fleet, including destroyers and cruisers.
A Backlog Of Challenges
Maintenance issues have consistently plagued the Navy. In August, the Government Accountability Office issued a report that found public shipyards only completed 11 percent of submarine maintenance periods on schedule.
Likewise, the Congressional Budget Office found in December 2025 that maintenance for the destroyer and amphibious fleets takes 20-100 percent longer than the Navy accounts for. The agency also estimated that destroyers will spend roughly nine years — or roughly a quarter of their planned service life — in maintenance.
When asked about maintenance delays resulting from lengthy deployments, Norfolk Naval Shipyard Commander Rear Adm. Kavon Hakimzadeh said during a September Center for Maritime Strategy roundtable that the situation is “going to be a pig through the snake kind of scenario.”
Hakimzadeh said there’s currently a “nice sequence” for aircraft carrier maintenance and that the service is targeting a six-month period for the Ford. He acknowledged that submarine maintenance is “a little bit of a different story,” and predicted destroyers would face the brunt of maintenance challenges upon returning from the Middle East.
“There’s some choke points just based on capacity out there for all the destroyers that are going to be coming back,” Hakimzadeh said. “We’re running the destroyers really hard out there, and I suspect they’re all going to need to go into the same dry dock, and we’re going to have to sequence them in.”
Eric Labs, a senior analyst for naval forces and weapons at the Congressional Budget Office, said the full impact of ongoing military operations on the fleet is difficult to predict because it’s unclear how long they will continue. However, he said the Navy has historically taken “at least several years” to catch up on maintenance after previous military operations that required a surge in naval capacity.
“At a general level, ships that are missing their maintenance availabilities now because of ongoing operations would have that maintenance manifest itself over the next several years,” Labs told Breaking Defense.
He noted that destroyers and aircraft carriers are most likely to be affected by deferred maintenance — destroyers due to their “high utilization,” and aircraft carriers because there are less than a dozen in the entire fleet and they are the Navy’s largest vessels.
While Labs said that some private maintenance shipyards that work on the Navy’s surface fleet have voiced concerns about a lack of work at present, he said they would face a hefty workload once destroyers return that would create planning and workforce challenges for both industry and the service.
“The private maintenance yards in the US are undergoing a famine and then, later, will experience a feast cycle,” Labs said. “The consequence of that will depend on unique ship circumstances. It could mean some ships will need to return to sea before getting all the maintenance they need, which could just exacerbate problems in the future. Or it could mean some ships will sit idle until the maintenance can be done.”
Even so, Labs said the impact would vary by ship — depending on its age, the length of its deployment, the timing of its last maintenance period and other factors.
Bradley Martin, a retired Navy captain who is now a senior policy researcher at RAND, also predicted it would take years for the fleet to recover from maintenance backlogs stemming from current operations in the Middle East. He said nearly every ship class would likely be affected, although the most acute maintenance issues could hit the destroyer fleet, given its heavy operational use in the Middle East.
“I think we’ll start seeing mounting cost as the Iran conflict winds down and might not see the full impact for at least two years,” Martin told Breaking Defense. “And it will be years past that before the force fully recovers.”

articles.title: Is the Finnish-Norwegian call with Putin a crack in Nordic resolve, or the start of a new path?
articles.snippet: Western European leaders have largely avoided speaking with Putin since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
articles.full_text:
STOCKHOLM and MILAN – A small fissure appears to have opened in the Nordic nations’ stance towards Russia, as the leaders of Norway and Finland held a rare call Tuesday with Russian president Vladimir Putin to discuss Ukraine.
While Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said the call was done with the blessing of Ukraine, it led to quick pushback from Denmark and caution from Sweden, underlining a key issue as Europe is in its fifth year of the Ukraine conflict — keeping nations aligned on how to handle Moscow.
“It was a 90-minute call. It was substantial and went into the issues. It was professional. There are large gaps in positions,” Norway’s Prime Minister Støre told the public broadcaster NRK after the conversation with Putin, adding that the call had been planned to be only 20 minutes in length.
“We stand by Ukraine and defend Ukraine’s right to defend itself. And we emphasize that there must be a diplomatic path to end this war in a lasting and just manner,” Støre said.
The joint phone call to Moscow was a follow-up to a meeting in Oslo one week earlier, where Stubb and Støre hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US special envoy Steve Witkoff. Representatives from several other countries, including Germany and Poland, were present at that meeting.
Western European leaders have largely avoided speaking with Putin since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The last notable contact by a European leader was French President Emmanuel Macron in July 2025, according to the BBC.
In a coordinated statement, Stubb said “The discussion was frank and substantive. We are neighbouring countries to Russia. The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions.”
In a statement on X, Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that Putin “stressed that a just and lasting peace can only be achieved if the Russian Federation’s legitimate interests are fully and unconditionally taken into account.” (The Financial Times reported that Putin spent most of the call complaining about Slavic history.)
Stubb and Støre stated that they took the call “as leaders of their respective countries and did not speak on behalf of Europe as a whole” — a point underlined by the response to the call from other parts of Europe.
Just after the communiqué was released by the president’s office in Helsinki, Copenhagen heavily criticised the initiative by its Nordic allies.“I am very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish solo initiative. It has not been coordinated with the rest of us,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told Danish TV 2.
“I believe we should keep Europe united instead of going it alone,” Frederiksen stressed.
Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who was in Helsinki for the Nordic Council’s annual session, said “My view is that everyone wants peace except Putin. I have rather low expectations for this kind of talks,” Kristersson said, according to the Swedish Daily DN, adding that he had not been briefed immediately on the outcome of discussions between Stubb, Støre and Putin.
Asked whether he considers it wise to hold talks with the Russian leader, Kristersson replied that it entirely depends on the outcome.
The Baltic leaders have so far been cautious in their comments. Estonia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna said that he had been briefed about the phone call to Moscow, according to the country’s public broadcaster ERR.
However, he stressed in a post on X that “Only increased pressure on Russia will make it take peace negotiations seriously” and that “Every contact with Russia must convey Europe’s unity and determination to support Ukraine and maintain pressure on Russia, while making clear that Europe will not negotiate away the fundamental principles underpinning its security.”
Coordination Or Individual Priorities?
The fact that it was Finland and Norway who made these calls should not be a major surprise, said Henri Vanhanen, a Finnish foreign-policy analyst, who emphasized in a post on X that the two share land borders with Russia.
Finland brings “long experience dealing with Russia, while Norway brings decades of expertise in security dialogue on the northern regions.” Stubb also has a “direct communication line” to Trump and both leaders have close ties with Zelenskyy.
“Norway is not part of the EU, but Finland is,” Vanhanen added. This duo can approach the issue as European NATO allies without having to decide on behalf of the entire EU who should represent Europe in the negotiations.”
Jim Townsend, a European expert with the Center for a New American Security, views the call as a first step in what could be a great role for Europe in negotiating a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Stubb, Townsend told Breaking Defense, is viewed as a pragmatic leader in Europe, who has good relations across the continent as well as in Washington. So it makes sense he would be taking the lead on these discussions, while Støre is viewed as largely in alignment with his Finnish counterpart.
As to the idea that this shows a crack in Europe’s alignment on Ukraine, Townsend pointed to the riots in France, the rise of the far-right in Germany and ongoing economic challenges across the continent as a sign that “there are cracks already” forming.
“Europe is hardly a unified monolith. I don’t read this so much as Europe cracking,” he noted. He added that, “some in Europe are trying to find a way out and beginning to say things publicly that they may have been only willing to say behind closed doors” about the need to find a way out of the Ukraine situation.
Nordic Alignment
The Nordic countries are among some of the NATO nations most directly exposed to the Russian threat: Finland shares a 1,340-kilometer (832.6-mile) land border with Russia; Norway borders it in the High North, near the important Kola Peninsula, that hosts Russian nuclear capabilities; and Sweden’s position in the Baltic Sea region makes it strategically important for the alliance’s northern flank.
According to Townsend, who formerly covered Europe as a Pentagon official, “It’s really the northern Europeans who have been the propellant for Ukraine,” and they have largely kept their alignment together to this point.
But that doesn’t mean everything is done the same, according to Maj. Gen. Johan Pekkari, the Swedish army chief, who talked to Breaking Defense at the AUSA conference in Washington earlier this month.
“Our dimensional threat will continue to be Russia,” Pekkari said. “I am sure we have the same view among the Nordic community, what may be a little different is how we pronounce it.”
His job is to “prepare for the worst case,” he said, which entails anticipating what such a scenario could look like.
Pekkari said that this kind of cooperation happens at all levels on a daily basis in Sweden and that sabotage is “part of what we anticipate in case of escalation,” noting that the country has prepared itself for by relying on “different tools.”
Tuija Karanko, the secretary general of the Finnish Defense and Aerospace Industries, which represents over 300 defense and dual-use technology companies, noted that when it comes to national security, the Finns sometimes go about it a different way.
“We definitely know what is going on and I would claim that we know it better than anybody else — the Finnish way is not to be very vocal about this, there is no need to go around and say what we think might happen,” Karanko told Breaking Defense at AUSA. “We know, are prepared and that is our mentality: Carry on and do your business.”
The acting chief of the Norwegian Army, Trond Nilsen, agreed with the points made by his counterparts about the common alignment that exists among the Nordic countries on the matter.
“We share the same borders, the same concerns, it is quite easy to speak to the Finns and Swedes because we are talking about the exact same thing. … The most important part for us is that the Norwegian Army is prepared for an invasion [if that took place],” he said at AUSA.
“The villain to fight is in Moscow. For a Norwegian, if you lost one or two battles you would withdraw and ask are we doing the right thing. … The Russians will not, they will just send more people,” he said.
He added that this is a scenario the country’s army needs to examine deeper.
“If you are sending a lot of [weapons with] warheads to the border, and attacking, we might stop the first wave but what about the second or third one? We are looking into this,” Nilsen said.
Aaron Mehta in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Moldova investigates possible foreign involvement in major government cyberattack
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said the incident may be part of a broader campaign targeting both citizens' personal data and government digital infrastructure, according to local media reports.
articles.full_text:
Moldova investigates possible foreign involvement in major government cyberattack
Moldova is investigating whether foreign state actors were involved in a major cyberattack on its government systems that exposed sensitive personal information and disrupted dozens of public services, the country's prime minister said Wednesday.
Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said the incident may be part of a broader campaign targeting both citizens' personal data and government digital infrastructure, according to local media reports.
"Our country is the target of coordinated and large-scale cyberattacks. We are not talking about an isolated incident," Tofan said, adding that authorities were examining the possible involvement of foreign state actors.
Moldova has not publicly attributed the attack to any country or hacking group.
Tofan's statement came a day after Moldova's Electronic Governance Agency (AGE) disclosed that hackers had exploited vulnerabilities in government services to extract large volumes of personal information between October 19 and 23.
The attackers made approximately 11 million requests to access data through government services. Preliminary findings indicate that information linked to about 750,000 identification numbers was extracted, although not every affected individual had all categories of personal data exposed.
The compromised information may include names, dates and places of birth, family relationships, health insurance status, social benefits, pensions, disability records, driver's licenses, photographs and vehicle ownership details.
Financial information, including bank account numbers, tax debts and government payment histories, may also have been accessed, according to the agency. Authorities said bank card information was not compromised and investigators had found no evidence that attackers had altered official government records.
According to the agency, the hackers exploited vulnerabilities in services that did not require authentication and used the information they obtained to extract additional data from interconnected government systems.
In response, authorities inspected 82 digital public services and temporarily disconnected those considered vulnerable, along with more than 30 government information systems and administrative panels.
The disruptions affected a range of public services, including online applications for construction permits, veterinary transport authorizations, medicine imports and food safety registrations, according to local media reports.
Most affected services have since been secured, and authorities are gradually restoring access following additional security checks, the agency said.
Authorities said they blocked unauthorized access on October 23 but detected additional attempts to breach government services on Sunday and Tuesday. Both attempts were unsuccessful.
The government warned that stolen information could be used in fraud schemes, including attempts to impersonate banks or public institutions to obtain passwords, authentication codes or money.
Government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said the incident could be part of a broader campaign of hybrid attacks against Moldova.
The country of approximately 2.4 million people, which borders Ukraine and Romania, has faced repeated cyberattacks and influence operations since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Moldovan authorities have previously accused Russia of conducting destabilization campaigns aimed at undermining state institutions and public confidence in the country's pro-European government under President Maia Sandu.
Daryna Antoniuk
is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: UK to look at making software companies liable for cyber breaches
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The new U.K. budget says the government will "consider where liability for cyber breaches should sit," potentially a landmark shift for a country that has relied on voluntary codes to encourage software vendors to improve security.
articles.full_text:
UK to look at making software companies liable for cyber breaches
The British government will consult on how to hold technology companies liable for cyber breaches caused by insecure products — potentially a landmark shift for a country that has for years relied on voluntary codes to encourage software vendors to improve security.
The commitment, made in budget documents published on Wednesday, comes amid growing alarm in Westminster over the economic damage caused by cyberattacks. Last year's hack of Jaguar Land Rover alone is estimated to have cost the British economy £1.9 billion ($2.5 billion).
According to the budget, the government “will consult next year on how to tackle insecure technology at source and consider where liability for cyber breaches should sit.” The work will build on an ongoing review of product liability law by the Law Commission of England and Wales.
Although the pledge occupies just one bullet point in the 166-page document, it marks the first formal pledge by a British government to examine where liability for cyber breaches should sit.
Significant questions remain, including which department will lead the consultation, when it will begin and whether ministers envisage a civil liability regime, statutory obligations on vendors, or both. HM Treasury did not respond to a request for comment.
One option likely to be considered internally is expanding the Product Security and Telecommunications Infrastructure (PSTI) Act, which since 2024 has imposed basic security requirements on manufacturers of consumer smart devices.
Officials are expected to ensure any new rules are compatible with the European Union’s own software cybersecurity regime, to avoid businesses facing heavy costs to comply with two separate sets of requirements.
The move follows years of pressure from Britain's own cybersecurity authorities, particularly Ollie Whitehouse, the chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the cyber and signals intelligence agency GCHQ.
The agency called publicly for a “strategic policy agenda” last year, after efforts to address insecure technology had stalled. Whitehouse had already warned, in a keynote address at the CyberUK conference in Birmingham in 2024, that the technology market was failing to reward companies for building resilient and secure products, while regulation and legislation struggled to keep pace.
Last year, he wrote that “the reality is that in 2025, we know how to build secure products and services” but “the business and commercial incentives to encourage adoption and sustainment of secure solutions are not sufficient.”
His argument echoed a debate in the United States, where proposals to make software makers liable for flawed code stalled for years amid disagreements over how to define the proper standard of care. The Trump administration has since rolled back several Biden-era secure-software requirements for federal suppliers.
The political pressure in Britain intensified last November, when the House of Commons Business and Trade Committee, chaired by Liam Byrne, said a lack of liability for software vendors was among the most pressing issues putting Britain’s economic and national security at risk.
It urged ministers to make the NCSC's voluntary software security code of practice legally binding, with penalties for companies that fail to comply.
Byrne described the Jaguar Land Rover attack as a “cyber shockwave ripping through our industrial heartlands,” while the committee warned of “a huge increase in the private ownership of public risk.”
The government's Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, introduced to Parliament that same month and now before the House of Lords, acknowledged some of the market failures identified by the NCSC in its impact assessment, which pointed to the “information asymmetry between vendors and buyers” making it difficult for customers to judge the security of the technologies they purchase.
In its current form, the legislation stops short of imposing obligations on software developers, concentrating instead on operators of critical infrastructure and their suppliers.
Arguments ahead
The European Union’s Cyber Resilience Act allows regulators to fine manufacturers of insecure products up to €15 million or 2.5% of global turnover, whichever is higher, with its main obligations taking effect in December 2027.
A separate overhaul of the bloc’s product liability rules, which member states must adopt by December, extends strict liability to software, including defects caused by missing security updates.
Attempts in Britain to shift liability onto software vendors are likely to face resistance, with the Business Software Alliance — whose members include Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon Web Services — having lobbied against such measures and argued that they would stifle innovation.
The proposals could also create friction with the United States, where the world’s largest technology vendors are based, and where successive administrations have regarded overseas regulatory efforts with suspicion when they appear to constrain the sector's commercial success.
In Britain, the Law Commission consultation referenced in the budget opened on October 8 and runs until January 14. It proposes broadening the definition of a “product” under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 to include software and AI systems, which currently sit in a legal gray area because the law was written for physical goods.
That review is sponsored by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, but responsibility for national cybersecurity policy now lies with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport. The country’s cyber minister, Baroness Lloyd, holds posts in both departments, as Recorded Future News previously reported.
£154 million for AI cyber defenses
Alongside the liability consultation, the budget commits £154 million ($205 million) in new funding for cyber defenses, much of which the Treasury had announced ahead of Wednesday's statement.
The largest allocation is £70 million ($93 million) for a National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre at the NCSC. The centre will, according to the budget, use artificial intelligence to identify vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and the wider economy.
The NCSC already scans internet-connected devices hosted in Britain, alerting organizations to exposed or vulnerable systems through its Early Warning and Proactive Notifications services. The budget does not explain how NERV will differ from those existing operations, and an agency spokesperson declined to comment.
A further £60 million ($79 million) will support the first phase of the NCSC’s Cyber Shield, announced in April as “a national scale, sovereign defense capability” that would use agentic AI systems to discover and fix cybersecurity weaknesses across government networks and critical national infrastructure.
Remaining funds will be used to strengthen the security of technology across the public sector, including systems operated by local authorities, hospitals and schools.
Separately, the government has allocated £40 million ($53 million) to establish a National Agentic Security Unit, tasked with detecting, investigating and responding to rogue AI agents.
The budget describes the unit’s ambitions as developing “world-first capabilities to detect and respond to misaligned agentic activity,” but does not identify which agency will host it nor how it will interact with similar projects associated with the NCSC.
The AI Security Institute, transferred to the Cabinet Office in July, will receive another £120 million ($159 million) over four years to expand its testing of frontier AI models.
The investments follow a week in which critical flaws in PHP, discovered using AI, forced websites offline around the world. The NCSC urged organizations to patch affected systems or consider taking them offline.
Alexander Martin
is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: Belarusian hackers increasingly acting as proxies for Russia amid war in Ukraine
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Belarus-linked hackers are increasingly aligning their cyber operations with Russia's interests in Ukraine, researchers said Wednesday.
articles.full_text:
Belarusian hackers increasingly acting as proxies for Russia amid war in Ukraine
Belarus-linked hackers are increasingly aligning their cyber operations with Russia's interests in Ukraine, the cybersecurity firm ESET said Wednesday.
Researchers have observed an "unprecedented operational convergence" between Russian and Belarusian hacking campaigns over the past few months.
"We observed increased and more assertive activity from Belarus-aligned threat actors, with their operations increasingly reflecting Russia's intelligence priorities in Ukraine in some areas," researchers said.
The most significant development came in late May, when a Belarus-linked hacking group launched a destructive cyberattack against a Ukrainian manufacturing company believed to play an important role in the country's transportation sector.
The attack was attributed to GhostWriter, a threat actor linked to Belarusian intelligence services that has previously conducted cyberespionage and influence operations against Ukraine, Poland and other countries in the region.
ESET said it was the first destructive cyberattack by a Belarus-aligned group that its researchers had documented in Europe, marking an escalation from the group's previously observed activities.
The hackers used data-wiping malware, which can erase information from compromised systems and disrupt their operations. ESET could not establish whether the malware was intended to cause damage or simply cover the tracks of an espionage operation.
Regardless of the hackers' motivation, the attack "sets a precedent" and raises the possibility that other Belarus-aligned state groups could carry out wiper attacks in the near future, researchers said.
Although Belarus has not deployed its own troops to fight in Ukraine, it has supported Russia's invasion by allowing Moscow to use its territory to launch military operations and missile strikes.
Belarusian hackers have historically focused on espionage and influence operations serving Minsk's own interests, but the latest destructive attack appeared more closely aligned with Russia's wartime priorities, according to ESET.
The researchers also identified several other Belarus-linked espionage operations targeting organizations of particular interest to Russia in connection with the war.
Researchers suggest that Belarusian hacking groups are increasingly serving as proxies or "force multipliers" for Russia. ESET warned that the trend could lead to closer cooperation between Russian and Belarusian hackers, including the sharing of tools and infrastructure, the outsourcing of targeting operations or even direct collaboration on cyberattacks.
North Korea's growing role
In addition to Belarus-linked groups, ESET found that North Korean hackers have stepped up their cyberattacks against Ukrainian targets amid growing military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow.
The researchers found some overlap between Moscow's and Pyongyang's intelligence interests, particularly regarding Ukraine's rapidly developing drone industry. However, researchers said the evidence of North Korean cyber operations directly supporting Russia's war effort was less definitive than the growing alignment they observed among Belarusian groups.
North Korean hackers have nevertheless expanded their targeting of Ukrainian organizations, potentially seeking intelligence and technical expertise that could benefit Pyongyang's own military capabilities.
Other cybersecurity researchers have also reported growing North Korean interest in Ukrainian targets.
Earlier in October, South Korean cybersecurity firm Genians said the North Korean hacking group Kimsuky had targeted Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security and international policy.
In May 2025, cybersecurity firm Proofpoint reported that North Korean-linked hackers had sent malicious emails to Ukrainian government agencies, potentially seeking intelligence about threats facing North Korean troops deployed alongside Russian forces.

is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

articles.title: FBI seizes ‘bulletproof’ hosting site accused of facilitating child abuse, money laundering
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The FBI seized the domain of a “bulletproof” hosting provider accused of facilitating a range of cybercrimes, including money laundering and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.
articles.full_text:
FBI seizes ‘bulletproof’ hosting site accused of facilitating child abuse, money laundering
The FBI seized the domain of a “bulletproof” hosting provider accused of facilitating a range of cybercrimes, including money laundering and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.
The Justice Department said Tuesday that a court authorized the seizure of virtualine.net — a service operating under names including Secury, Massgod, Spamhouse, Lanedo and Omegatech — which has now been replaced by a splashpage.
So-called “bulletproof” hosting providers are specialized criminal businesses that rent critical infrastructure to customers based on the promise they will ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.
According to court records, Virtualine explicitly advertised on cybercrime forums, offering hosting for “all illegal/black hat activities,” including phishing, carding and spam. Although the provider claimed to prohibit customers involved in terrorism or child abuse material, prosecutors allege it did not enforce those restrictions.
In June 2025, Virtualine boasted on HackForums that it had “ignored more abuse than your last three therapists.”
In January, about a month after allegedly providing an IP address to a forum used to sell sexually explicit images of minors, distribute nonconsensual intimate images and advertise account-hacking services, the company was sent complaints from authorities in Germany, Canada and Australia, as well as the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children and a victim’s attorney.
Instead of terminating services to the forum, Virtualine helped its operators build another site for uploading and downloading illicit content, according to the Justice Department. The site remained online despite complaints related to sexually explicit images of children.
Virtualine accepted bitcoin payments through a service it named “BTC [NO-AML],” referencing anti-money laundering checks. Prosecutors said Virtualine attempted to launder the proceeds to conceal their origin, though some payments were traceable to criminal groups.
The FBI’s Washington Field Office led the investigation, assisted by authorities in Germany, the Netherlands and Britain, along with private sector partners OverRIPE and Lumen. The Justice Department did not identify Virtualine’s operators or announce criminal charges at the time of the domain seizure.
The seizure follows a series of international actions against bulletproof hosting providers, particularly Russia-linked services accused of supporting ransomware gangs.
In February 2025, the U.S., UK and Australia sanctioned Zservers for allegedly supporting the LockBit ransomware gang. Dutch police seized 127 of its servers that same week.
The U.S. Treasury Department sanctioned Russia-based Aeza Group in July 2025 for allegedly hosting the BianLian ransomware gang and information-stealing malware. Researchers also linked the provider to the Doppelgänger disinformation campaign.
In November, the three countries sanctioned Media Land over alleged ties to the LockBit, BlackSuit and Play ransomware groups. U.S. prosecutors had charged three alleged operators in that case, which they said resulted in about $62 million in victim losses.
Dutch authorities arrested two men and seized 800 servers in May during an investigation into infrastructure linked to Stark Industries, an EU-sanctioned provider accused of enabling Russian cyber operations. Investigators said another company took over Stark's infrastructure after sanctions were imposed.
The long-term impact of such crackdowns has been questioned. Threat intelligence firm Intel 471 reported in August that disruptions had driven customers to newer providers operated by former resellers, fragmenting the market rather than eliminating demand.

is the UK Editor for Recorded Future News. He was previously a technology reporter for Sky News and a fellow at the European Cyber Conflict Research Initiative, now Virtual Routes. He can be reached securely using Signal on: AlexanderMartin.79

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

articles.title: Nefilim, Hive ransomware operator given five-year-plus sentence after guilty plea
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Ukrainian national Artem Stryzhak, 36, had pleaded guilty last year to charges related to participating in at least two well-known ransomware groups.
articles.full_text:
Nefilim, Hive ransomware operator given five-year-plus sentence after guilty plea
A former ransomware hacker was sentenced to 70 months in prison after pleading guilty last year to charges tied to several cyberattacks on hospitals, government entities and more.
Artem Stryzhak, a 36-year-old from Ukraine, was an affiliate of the Nefilim ransomware group while living in Barcelona, Spain. Throughout 2021, Stryzhak used Nefilim to launch attacks on organizations in the U.S., Canada and Australia.
Stryzhak paid Nefilim administrators, including indicted co-conspirator Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a 20% fee of all ransoms extorted from victims. Stryzhak eventually moved on from Nefilim and joined the Hive ransomware gang — working with the group from October 2021 to January 2023. Tymoshchuk has evaded capture.
Stryzhak helped Hive attack organizations throughout the COVID-19 pandemic, targeting hospitals, governments and businesses. The group encrypted thousands of victims across 80 countries and earned millions in ransom payments throughout its run as a prominent ransomware gang.
“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Assistant FBI Director Brett Leatherman. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses.”
Prosecutors listed one incident where a hospital was unable to accept new patients during the pandemic due to a Hive ransomware attack. The Hive ransomware gang was disrupted by the FBI after a months-long operation.
Stryzhak was eventually arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited last April. He pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.
“This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyberattacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva.
Prosecutors said they are still searching for Tymoshchuk, who is also accused of being an administrator for the LockerGoga and MegaCortex ransomware gangs.
U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. said they “remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk.”
The DOJ previously issued an $11 million reward for information on Tymoshchuk’s whereabouts and a $15 million reward for information on other members of Hive.
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
